<div class="soco-reg-hero">
<div class="soco-reg-hero-inner">
<div class="soco-reg-eyebrow">
<p>Society of Cutaneous Oncology · Proposed Meeting · Fall 2026</p>
</div>
<h1 id="inside-the-review-room">Inside the Review Room</h1>
<div class="soco-reg-subtitle">
<p><strong>From patient-level data to FDA regulatory
decision-making</strong> — a proposed 90-minute, moderator-led panel on
how oncology evidence is reviewed, reconstructed, debated, and
ultimately translated into regulatory action.</p>
</div>
<div class="soco-reg-tags">
<p><span class="soco-reg-tag">Regulatory medicine</span> <span class="soco-reg-tag">Patient-level data</span> <span class="soco-reg-tag">Benefit–risk</span> <span class="soco-reg-tag">Advisory
committees</span> <span class="soco-reg-tag">Moderated discussion</span></p>
</div>
</div>
</div>
<div class="soco-reg-shell">
<section id="the-idea" class="soco-reg-card">
<h2>Meeting concept</h2>
<p>Recent regulatory discussions in cutaneous oncology have highlighted
an important gap between how clinicians encounter clinical-trial
evidence and how FDA reviewers evaluate the same evidence. A publication
may present a clean summary estimate; a regulatory review may involve
reconstruction of patient-level efficacy and safety data, adjudication
of discrepancies, sensitivity analyses, multidisciplinary debate, and a
different evidentiary question altogether.</p>
<p>The proposed meeting would <strong>not be a retrospective debate
about a particular application</strong>. The RP1 experience is better
used as the prompt for a broader educational question:</p>
<div class="soco-reg-quote">
<p>What actually happens inside FDA between receipt of an oncology
application and a regulatory decision — and when does an advisory
committee become part of that process?</p>
</div>
<p>The goal would be to make the review process visible to practicing
clinicians and investigators, with particular attention to the parts
that are usually hidden from view: <strong>patient-level data review,
independent analyses, multidisciplinary deliberation, and the role of
advisory committees.</strong></p>
</section>
<div class="soco-reg-grid-3">
<div class="soco-reg-mini">
<div class="soco-reg-mini-label">
<p>Format</p>
</div>
<div class="soco-reg-mini-value">
<p>Conversational, moderator-led panel</p>
</div>
</div>
<div class="soco-reg-mini">
<div class="soco-reg-mini-label">
<p>Duration</p>
</div>
<div class="soco-reg-mini-value">
<p>90 minutes</p>
</div>
</div>
<div class="soco-reg-mini">
<div class="soco-reg-mini-label">
<p>Proposed panel</p>
</div>
<div class="soco-reg-mini-value">
<p>FDA regulatory medicine colleagues, with a SoCO moderator</p>
</div>
</div>
</div>
<section id="proposed-format" class="soco-reg-card">
<h2>Proposed format</h2>
<p>The session would be structured as a <strong>conversational,
moderator-led panel rather than a series of formal presentations</strong>.
One or two simple orienting slides could be useful — for example, a
schematic of the review pathway and a schematic of what an application
contains — but the discussion would otherwise move through moderator
questions, dialogue between the panelists, and audience discussion.</p>
<p>Moderator questions would be shared in advance so the discussion
can stay focused on <strong>process and general principles</strong>,
while still leaving room for give-and-take between the panelists and the
audience. The intent would not be to ask the speakers to discuss
confidential deliberations or re-litigate a specific product decision.</p>
</section>
<section id="minute-agenda" class="soco-reg-card">
<h2>Proposed 90-minute agenda</h2>
<div class="soco-reg-act">
<p><small>Act I · approximately 50 minutes</small> <strong>Inside the
FDA Review Room</strong></p>
</div>
<p><strong><span class="soco-reg-time">0–5 min</span> Opening and
framing</strong><br />
Why this matters to clinicians: the difference between reading a paper
and reviewing an application.</p>
<p><strong><span class="soco-reg-time">5–15 min</span> What actually arrives at
FDA?</strong><br />
What an oncology application contains, what is available at the patient
level, and how regulatory evidence differs from the final
manuscript.</p>
<p><strong><span class="soco-reg-time">15–28 min</span> Who reviews the
application?</strong><br />
How the work moves from individual discipline review through
multidisciplinary discussion, supervisory review, office-level
deliberation, and Center-level decision-making.</p>
<p><strong><span class="soco-reg-time">28–45 min</span> Reconstructing the
evidence</strong><br />
The centerpiece of the session: how efficacy and safety are
independently interrogated, how reviewers work with patient-level data,
and what happens when FDA and sponsor analyses do not align.</p>
<p><strong><span class="soco-reg-time">45–55 min</span> From analysis to
regulatory action</strong><br />
How unresolved questions become information requests, additional
analyses, labeling discussions, benefit–risk judgments, approval, or a
complete response.</p>
<div class="soco-reg-act">
<p><small>Act II · approximately 25 minutes</small> <strong>When the
Review Goes Public: Advisory Committees</strong></p>
</div>
<p><strong><span class="soco-reg-time">55–65 min</span> Why convene an advisory
committee?</strong><br />
Who initiates the process, what kinds of uncertainty lead to outside
consultation, and how FDA decides what it wants the committee to
address.</p>
<p><strong><span class="soco-reg-time">65–77 min</span> Inside the
meeting</strong><br />
How questions are built, discussion versus voting questions, what the
review team listens for, and how the public meeting fits into an already
mature internal review.</p>
<p><strong><span class="soco-reg-time">77–80 min</span> The morning
after</strong><br />
How the committee’s advice is interpreted and incorporated into the
ongoing regulatory process.</p>
<p><strong><span class="soco-reg-time">80–90 min</span> Audience discussion +
closing question</strong><br />
How should clinicians interpret an FDA review, a product label, and a
peer-reviewed manuscript as different windows onto the same trial?</p>
</section>
<section id="moderator-question-bank" class="soco-reg-card">
<h2>Moderator question bank</h2>
<h3 id="act-i-inside-the-fda-review-room">Act I — Inside the FDA Review
Room</h3>
<section id="what-actually-comes-through-the-door" class="soco-reg-question-group">
<h3>1 · What actually comes through the door?</h3>
<ul>
<li>When a sponsor submits a BLA or NDA, what does the clinical review
team actually receive?</li>
<li>At the patient level, what information is available beyond the
sponsor’s tables and figures?</li>
<li>How standardized are the submitted datasets, and how much work is
required before a reviewer can interrogate them?</li>
<li>What can a reviewer inspect when an individual patient looks unusual
— dates, narratives, adverse events, concomitant therapy, imaging
assessments, protocol deviations, or other source-level
information?</li>
<li>How different is the evidence package available to FDA from the
evidence package that clinicians eventually encounter in a
publication?</li>
</ul>
</section>
<section id="who-actually-reviews-the-data" class="soco-reg-question-group">
<h3>2 · Who actually reviews the data?</h3>
<ul>
<li>Who is responsible for the first-pass clinical review of efficacy
and safety?</li>
<li>What is the division of labor between clinical reviewers,
statisticians, pharmacologists, safety reviewers, regulatory project
managers, and other disciplines?</li>
<li>Who is actually writing code or reproducing analyses, and who is
looking at individual patients?</li>
<li>How often do clinical and statistical reviewers arrive at different
interpretations of the same signal?</li>
<li>How are disagreements handled within the multidisciplinary review
team?</li>
<li>At what points does the review move from an individual reviewer to
team-level, office-level, and Center-level discussion?</li>
</ul>
</section>
<section id="what-does-fda-independently-reviewed-the-data-actually-mean" class="soco-reg-question-group">
<h3>3 · What does “FDA independently reviewed the data” actually
mean?</h3>
<ul>
<li>If a sponsor reports an objective response rate, progression-free
survival estimate, or safety event rate, how independently does FDA
reproduce that number?</li>
<li>Does FDA effectively construct its own analytic version of the trial
from the submitted patient-level data?</li>
<li>Which analyses are routinely reproduced, and which are generally
accepted from the sponsor unless a concern emerges?</li>
<li>How are evaluability, missing assessments, censoring, progression
dates, response confirmation, protocol deviations, and analysis
populations handled?</li>
<li>What happens when the sponsor’s estimate and FDA’s estimate
differ?</li>
<li>How large or consequential does a discrepancy need to be before it
changes the regulatory conversation?</li>
<li>Is the key issue usually the numerical difference itself, or what
the discrepancy reveals about uncertainty in the underlying
evidence?</li>
</ul>
</section>
<section id="following-one-patient-down-the-rabbit-hole" class="soco-reg-question-group">
<h3>4 · Following one patient down the rabbit hole</h3>
<ul>
<li>What makes a reviewer stop at an individual patient and investigate
more deeply?</li>
<li>How much manual patient-level review occurs in a modern
application?</li>
<li>Can a single patient materially change the interpretation of an
efficacy endpoint or a safety signal?</li>
<li>How are ambiguous cases adjudicated across clinical and statistical
reviewers?</li>
<li>When FDA asks the sponsor for clarification, what does that exchange
look like in practice?</li>
<li>How often does a patient-level discrepancy lead to a broader
re-analysis of the dataset?</li>
</ul>
</section>
<section id="from-analysis-to-a-regulatory-judgment" class="soco-reg-question-group">
<h3>5 · From analysis to a regulatory judgment</h3>
<ul>
<li>At what point does the review move from “What does the dataset
show?” to “Is the benefit–risk profile sufficient for approval?”</li>
<li>How is uncertainty carried into that benefit–risk judgment?</li>
<li>How are different disciplinary reviews synthesized into a single
regulatory position?</li>
<li>What kinds of unresolved issues can be addressed through labeling,
postmarketing commitments, or additional analyses — and what kinds of
issues are fundamental enough to prevent approval?</li>
<li>How does a complete response letter fit into the broader review
process?</li>
<li>When an application returns after a complete response, what is
effectively reopened and what prior work carries forward?</li>
</ul>
</section>
<h3 id="act-ii-when-the-review-goes-public-advisory-committees">Act II —
When the Review Goes Public: Advisory Committees</h3>
<section id="why-does-an-application-go-to-an-advisory-committee" class="soco-reg-question-group">
<h3>6 · Why does an application go to an advisory committee?</h3>
<ul>
<li>Who first raises the possibility of an advisory committee, and who
ultimately decides to convene one?</li>
<li>At what stage of the review is that decision usually made?</li>
<li>What kinds of problems are best suited to outside expert advice:
scientific uncertainty, disagreement about benefit–risk, novel
technology, precedent-setting questions, or something else?</li>
<li>Does referral to an advisory committee imply that the internal
review team is divided, or can it occur even when the team has a fairly
developed view?</li>
<li>What does FDA hope to learn from an advisory committee that it
cannot obtain from its internal review alone?</li>
</ul>
</section>
<section id="how-are-the-committee-questions-created" class="soco-reg-question-group">
<h3>7 · How are the committee questions created?</h3>
<ul>
<li>Who writes the questions that ultimately appear in the briefing
documents and at the meeting?</li>
<li>How does FDA decide whether it wants a discussion question, a formal
vote, or both?</li>
<li>What makes a good voting question from the regulatory team’s
perspective?</li>
<li>How much should observers infer from the wording of FDA’s
questions?</li>
<li>By the time the advisory committee meets, how mature is the internal
review team’s thinking?</li>
</ul>
</section>
<section id="what-does-the-review-team-hear-that-the-audience-may-miss" class="soco-reg-question-group">
<h3>8 · What does the review team hear that the audience may miss?</h3>
<ul>
<li>Is the numerical vote the most important output, or is the
discussion often more informative?</li>
<li>How does the team interpret a strongly favorable vote with important
reservations? A divided vote? A unanimous vote with substantial
uncertainty?</li>
<li>What kinds of comments from committee members can materially change
the team’s thinking?</li>
<li>How should clinicians understand the fact that the committee is
advisory rather than determinative?</li>
</ul>
</section>
<section id="what-happens-the-next-morning" class="soco-reg-question-group">
<h3>9 · What happens the next morning?</h3>
<ul>
<li>Does the review team formally reconvene after the advisory
committee?</li>
<li>How is the committee’s advice incorporated into the remaining
review?</li>
<li>Can the meeting change the requested analyses, labeling discussions,
postmarketing requirements, or ultimate regulatory recommendation?</li>
<li>When FDA ultimately reaches a conclusion that differs from the
committee vote, what is the best way for clinicians to understand that
apparent divergence?</li>
</ul>
</section>
</section>
<section id="closing-discussion" class="soco-reg-card">
<h2>Closing discussion</h2>
<p>A final synthesis could return to the question that motivated the
session:</p>
<div class="soco-reg-quote">
<p>Why might FDA and a peer-reviewed publication describe the same
clinical trial differently without either necessarily being “wrong”?</p>
</div>
<p>Possible threads:</p>
<ul>
<li>different data cuts or analysis populations;</li>
<li>independent reconstruction of efficacy or safety outcomes;</li>
<li>different handling of missing data, censoring, evaluability, or
protocol deviations;</li>
<li>sensitivity analyses that matter more in a regulatory review than in
a manuscript;</li>
<li>regulatory benefit–risk questions that are not identical to the
scientific question posed in a publication;</li>
<li>the difference between summarizing a trial and deciding whether the
evidence supports a particular regulatory action.</li>
</ul>
<p>The take-home message would be that the <strong>FDA review, product
label, and peer-reviewed manuscript are related but distinct views of
the evidence</strong> — each generated for a different purpose.</p>
</section>

      <span class="soco-feedback-summary-copy">

        class="soco-feedback-form"
        name="soco-inside-review-room-feedback"
        method="POST"
        data-netlify="true"
        netlify-honeypot="bot-field"
        id="soco-inside-review-room-feedback"
      >
        <input type="hidden" name="form-name" value="soco-inside-review-room-feedback">
        <input type="hidden" name="meeting_title" value="Inside the Review Room">
        <input type="hidden" name="meeting_url" id="soco-review-room-meeting-url" value="">

        </p>

<script>
(function () {
  const form = document.getElementById("soco-inside-review-room-feedback");
  const urlField = document.getElementById("soco-review-room-meeting-url");
  const status = document.getElementById("soco-review-feedback-status");

  if (urlField) urlField.value = window.location.href;
  if (!form) return;

  form.addEventListener("submit", async function (event) {
    event.preventDefault();

    const submitButton = form.querySelector('button[type="submit"]');
    const originalLabel = submitButton ? submitButton.textContent : "";

    if (submitButton) {
      submitButton.disabled = true;
      submitButton.textContent = "Sending…";
    }

    if (status) {
      status.classList.remove("is-visible");
      status.textContent = "";
    }

    try {
      const formData = new FormData(form);
      const encoded = new URLSearchParams();

      for (const [key, value] of formData.entries()) {
        encoded.append(key, value);
      }

      const response = await fetch("/", {
        method: "POST",
        headers: { "Content-Type": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded" },
        body: encoded.toString()
      });

      if (!response.ok) throw new Error("Submission failed");

      const firstName = (formData.get("name") || "").toString().trim().split(/\s+/)[0];
      form.reset();
      if (urlField) urlField.value = window.location.href;

      if (status) {
        status.textContent = firstName
          ? `Thank you, ${firstName}. Your thoughts have been received.`
          : "Thank you. Your thoughts have been received.";
        status.classList.add("is-visible");
      }

      if (submitButton) submitButton.textContent = "Sent";
    } catch (error) {
      if (status) {
        status.textContent = "We could not send your response just now. Please try again.";
        status.classList.add("is-visible");
      }

      if (submitButton) {
        submitButton.disabled = false;
        submitButton.textContent = originalLabel;
      }
      return;
    }

    if (submitButton) {
      setTimeout(function () {
        submitButton.disabled = false;
        submitButton.textContent = originalLabel;
      }, 1600);
    }
  });
})();
</script>

</div>
